beginner: Cabbage grows best in rich, well-drained soil with plenty of compost mixed in, and it likes steady, even moisture. Keep the water consistent: a big swing from dry to soaking wet near harvest makes the heads split. Soil that holds moisture but drains well is ideal.
seasoned: Cabbage is a heavy feeder that rewards a fertile, well-drained loam high in organic matter held at even moisture. Work in compost before planting, and aim for a moisture-retentive but well-draining bed, since both waterlogging (which invites root maggot and rots) and drought stress hurt heading. The signature cabbage soil issue is uneven water near maturity: a sudden flush of water into a firm head bursts it, so steady moisture matters most as the heads fill. Clubroot, the key brassica soil disease, is far more likely in acidic, poorly drained ground.

beginner: Cabbage grows best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about 6.0 to 7.0. A simple soil test tells you where you stand. If you have had clubroot, a soil disease, keeping the soil closer to neutral (up toward 7.0 or a bit above) helps hold it back.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0 (UMN and Iowa State both give 6 to 7; Clemson lists 5.8 to 6.5). Cabbage tolerates a wider 5.5 to 7.5 band. Clubroot, the major brassica soil disease, is far more likely in acidic soil below about 6.5, so where it is a concern lime acidic ground well ahead of planting and hold the pH toward neutral or slightly above.

beginner: Cabbage needs rich soil and regular feeding to grow a big, solid head. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then feed with a nitrogen fertilizer once the plants take off and again as the heads start to form. Keep the watering even, because a lot of fertilizer plus a sudden soaking can crack the heads.
seasoned: Cabbage is a heavy feeder that needs steady nitrogen to build a large, solid head. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-10 or 10-10-10 into the bed before planting (Clemson: 5-10-10 at 3 pounds per 100 square feet), then side-dress with nitrogen once the plants are established and again as heads begin to cup, using about 34-0-0 or calcium nitrate. Keep nitrogen steady through heading, but pair it with even moisture: a late surge of growth from heavy feeding plus a sudden drink of water is what splits heads.

beginner: Time to feed your cabbage.
seasoned: Time to side-dress your cabbage with nitrogen as the heads begin to form.

beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then a nitrogen feed once the plants take off and again as heads form.
seasoned: High N to build a large, solid head: a 5-10-10 or 10-10-10 starter worked in before planting, then a nitrogen side-dress such as 34-0-0 or calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) as the plants establish and begin to head.

beginner: Follow the label rate for a balanced vegetable fertilizer at planting, then a nitrogen feed beside the plants as heads start.
seasoned: Work in 5-10-10 at about 3 pounds per 100 square feet before planting, then side-dress with about 1 pound of 34-0-0 (or 2 pounds of calcium nitrate) per 100 feet of row as heads begin to form, watered in alongside the plants.

beginner: Cabbage does well next to aromatic herbs, onions, and quick crops you can tuck in while the plants are small. The most important rule is to keep it away from other cabbage-family plants, which share the same pests and diseases.
seasoned: Most cabbage companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested. The ones worth acting on are practical: aromatic herbs and alliums as scent-based deterrents for cabbage pests, small flowering plants such as sweet alyssum and dill to draw the parasitic wasps and hoverflies that attack cabbage aphids and caterpillars (a habitat tactic Clemson recommends for cole crops), and quick crops like lettuce that use the open ground while the cabbage fills in. The well-grounded caution is to separate cabbage from other brassicas, which share clubroot and the whole cabbage-family pest complex, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect.

beginner: Sweet alyssum makes lots of tiny flowers that bring in helpful insects which eat aphids and caterpillars, two major cabbage pests.
seasoned: Sweet alyssum is one of the better-supported cabbage companions. Its low mats of tiny flowers are a classic insectary plant, drawing the hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitic wasps that prey on cabbage aphids and the cabbage-family caterpillars, and Clemson specifically advises small flowers like alyssum near cole crops for biological control. Let it self-sow along the bed edge.

beginner: Dill's flowers attract helpful insects that hunt the aphids and caterpillars that bother cabbage.
seasoned: Dill works for cabbage mainly through beneficial insects. Its umbel flowers draw the parasitoid wasps and hoverflies that attack cabbage aphids and cabbageworms, and Clemson lists dill among the flowers to plant near cole crops for natural control. Let some flower, and keep it off to the side so it does not shade the heads.

beginner: Onions are a traditional neighbor for cabbage; their strong smell is said to help confuse and deter cabbage pests.
seasoned: Alliums are a traditional brassica companion, their pungent scent thought to mask the crop from the cabbage pests that hunt partly by smell. Shallow-rooted and undemanding, onions tuck around young cabbage without competing for much. Treat it as a low-risk, scent-based aid rather than a proven control.

beginner: Keep cabbage away from other cabbage-family plants like broccoli, brussels sprouts, kale, and cauliflower. They share the same pests and diseases, so grouping them makes problems worse.
seasoned: Planting cabbage shoulder to shoulder with its brassica relatives, broccoli, brussels sprouts, cauliflower, kale, collards, concentrates the family's shared pests (cabbage aphids, cabbageworms, loopers, harlequin bugs, root maggots) and shared diseases in one spot, and repeated same-family planting lets soil-borne clubroot and Fusarium yellows build up. Spread brassicas out and rotate where they grow each year.

beginner: You'll see ragged holes chewed in the leaves, green caterpillars on the plant, and dark droppings, and worst of all, caterpillars and their mess tunneled down inside the head where they are hard to wash out.
seasoned: Ragged holes chewed in the wrapper leaves with green caterpillars and dark frass; as heads form, larvae bore inside and foul them, the costly damage. Imported cabbageworms are velvety green; cabbage loopers move in a looping arch; diamondback larvae are small and wriggle when disturbed (Clemson rates the diamondback the most numerous cole-crop caterpillar in home gardens).

beginner: These are caterpillars that hatch from eggs laid by white butterflies and small moths. They love cabbage-family plants, chew the leaves, and bore into the head you want to eat.
seasoned: The larvae of the imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth feed on brassica foliage and penetrate the head; the adults are white or brownish butterflies and moths that lay eggs on the leaves. Cabbage is a primary host for all three.

beginner: Spray Bt, which is safe and targets only caterpillars, or spinosad, and pick caterpillars and eggs off by hand from under the leaves. Spray again after rain, since it washes off.
seasoned: Spray Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) or spinosad, which target caterpillars and spare beneficials, and hand-pick larvae and eggs from leaf undersides. Repeat after rain, since Bt breaks down. Tighten control as heads cup, when damage to the head is the expensive kind.

beginner: Cover plants with a light fabric row cover after planting to keep the butterflies and moths from laying eggs, clear away old cabbage-family plants, and watch for the first white butterflies as your signal to act.
seasoned: Use floating row cover or fine mesh from transplanting to exclude the egg-laying adults, clean up brassica debris that shelters pupae, and scout for the first white butterflies as a spray cue.

beginner: You'll see clusters of small gray-green insects with a dusty, waxy coating on the new growth and tucked into the folds of the head, where they are very hard to wash out. Leaves may curl and there can be a sticky film.
seasoned: The gray-green, waxy-coated cabbage aphid forms dense colonies on growing tips and leaf undersides and then lodges in the folds of the developing head, where it contaminates the marketable product with insects and honeydew and is very hard to clean at harvest. Curling and distortion of young leaves is common.

beginner: Cabbage aphids are tiny insects that suck the plant's juices and breed fast. They love cabbage and hide down in the head, which is the part you eat.
seasoned: Brevicoryne brassicae, a brassica-specialist aphid, sucks sap and reproduces rapidly; contamination of the harvested head with aphids and sticky honeydew is usually the real problem rather than plant stunting. Pressure is heaviest on the long-season fall crop.

beginner: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water and hit the undersides of leaves with insecticidal soap or neem oil, repeating every few days. Welcome ladybugs and lacewings, which eat aphids.
seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap, neem, or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides; repeat every few days. Conserve natural enemies (the parasitoid Diaeretiella rapae, hoverflies, ladybugs) that suppress this aphid.

beginner: Check the growing tips and the developing head often and act early. Go easy on nitrogen once heads form, since soft growth draws them, and clear away old cabbage-family plants after harvest.
seasoned: Scout growing tips and the head weekly and catch infestations before aphids colonize the head. Avoid excess nitrogen once heads set, use row cover on young plants, and destroy crop debris that carries them over.

beginner: New transplants wilt and grow badly or fall over. If you pull one up, you'll find small white maggots eating the roots. It is worst in cool, wet soil.
seasoned: Transplants wilt, grow poorly, and may collapse; pulling a plant reveals small white maggots tunneling in the roots and lower stem. Damage is worst in cool, wet soil at spring establishment.

beginner: A small fly lays eggs at the base of the plant, and the maggots that hatch burrow down and eat the roots. The fly is most active in cool, damp weather, so spring transplants are most at risk.
seasoned: The larvae of the cabbage root fly (Delia radicum) tunnel into brassica roots; the adult lays eggs at the stem base, and the maggots feed below, sometimes killing young plants and opening the door to rots.

beginner: Once the maggots are in the roots you can't save that plant, so pull and throw away the badly damaged ones. Put your effort into protecting the rest from new eggs.
seasoned: There is no effective rescue once maggots are in the roots; remove and destroy badly affected plants and protect the rest from further egg-laying.

beginner: Put a small collar or disk around the base of each transplant to stop the fly from laying eggs there, or use a row cover. Avoid planting into cold, soggy soil, and rotate away from where cabbage-family plants grew.
seasoned: Place a collar or disk around the stem base at transplanting to block egg-laying, or use row cover; avoid planting into cold, wet soil and rotate away from where brassicas grew.

beginner: Shield-shaped black-and-orange (or black-and-red) bugs on the leaves, which develop white or yellow spots, then brown and look tattered. It is mostly a warm-region problem and loves cabbage-family plants.
seasoned: Shield-shaped bugs up to about 3/8 inch, brightly black-and-yellow or black-and-red, feeding with piercing-sucking mouthparts that leave white stipples; affected leaves brown and look tattered, and heavy feeding wilts and deforms plants. A warm-region brassica specialist.

beginner: The harlequin bug is a colorful stink-bug relative that pierces the leaves and sucks the juices, leaving pale blotches. It strongly prefers cabbage-family plants, especially in the South.
seasoned: The harlequin bug (Murgantia histrionica) is a true bug that specializes on cole crops, most damaging in the southern United States, where it completes several generations a year and overwinters as an adult in debris and weeds.

beginner: Search out and crush the bugs, their barrel-shaped eggs laid in rows, and the young ones by hand. Use a row cover to keep them off, pull badly infested plants, and clear away weeds and old plants where they hide over winter.
seasoned: Hand-pick and crush adults, nymphs, and the barrel-shaped egg rows; exclude with floating row cover; remove heavily infested plants. Insecticidal soap, pyrethrum, or neem help where pressure is severe.

beginner: Clean up garden debris and cabbage-family weeds where the adults overwinter, use row cover, and consider a trap crop of mustard to lure them away from the main crop, then destroy it.
seasoned: Eliminate overwintering sites by removing crop debris and crucifer weeds, use row cover, and deploy an early trap crop of mustard to divert overwintering adults, then destroy it before the main crop is set out.

beginner: Lots of tiny round holes in the leaves of young plants, made by small dark beetles that jump away like fleas when you get close. Bad damage can stunt seedlings.
seasoned: Tiny round shot-hole pits chewed in the leaves of young plants; the small dark beetles jump like fleas when disturbed. Heavy feeding stunts or kills seedlings and slows establishment.

beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew on young cabbage-family leaves. They hurt seedlings most, because a tiny plant can't grow fast enough to recover.
seasoned: Flea beetles chew the foliage of young brassicas and are most damaging at the seedling stage; a vigorous transplant generally outgrows them, but a stalled seedling can be set back badly.

beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover, and if there are a lot of beetles, use a spray such as spinosad. The main goal is to get the seedlings big enough to handle the damage.
seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover and spray spinosad if pressure is high; the goal is getting plants past the vulnerable seedling stage.

beginner: Cover seedlings with row cover from the start, keep them strong with steady water and food so they grow past the damage, and pull nearby weeds in the cabbage family.
seasoned: Use row cover from transplanting, keep seedlings vigorous with even water and feeding so they grow through the damage, and clean up weedy brassica relatives nearby.

beginner: Plants wilt in the afternoon, stay small and yellowish, and don't bounce back. If you dig one up, the roots are swollen into lumpy, club-shaped knobs.
seasoned: Plants wilt in the heat of the day, grow stunted and yellowed, and recover poorly; roots are swollen into distorted clubs and galls instead of normal fine roots.

beginner: A germ that lives in the soil infects the roots of cabbage-family plants and makes them swell, which stops the plant from taking up water and food. It stays in the soil for years.
seasoned: A soilborne organism (Plasmodiophora brassicae) infects brassica roots and forms the galls, which block water and nutrient uptake. It persists in soil for many years, spreads in contaminated soil and water, and infects most readily in acidic soils below pH 6.5.

beginner: There's no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. Keeping the soil from being too acidic (closer to neutral) helps hold it back, and growing cabbage-family plants only rarely in that spot starves the germ out.
seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy them. Raising soil pH toward neutral with lime suppresses the disease, and long rotations starve it out over time.

beginner: Don't grow cabbage or other cabbage-family plants in the same spot more than once every few years, longer if you've had clubroot. Keep the soil from being too acidic, improve drainage, and clean soil off your tools.
seasoned: Rotate brassicas out of affected ground on a long cycle (UMN advises up to 7 years where clubroot is known), keep soil pH up, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil on tools and boots.

beginner: Yellow patches shaped like the letter V appear at the leaf edges, pointing inward, with black veins inside them. It can spread through the plant and rot the head.
seasoned: Yellow, V-shaped lesions spread inward from the leaf margins, with the veins inside the V turning black; the disease moves through the vascular system and can blacken and rot the head. Often the most serious cabbage disease in warm, wet weather.

beginner: A bacteria that often comes in on infected seeds or transplants. It gets into the leaves and travels through the plant's veins, spreading fastest in warm, wet weather.
seasoned: A seedborne bacterium (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris) that enters through leaf pores and wounds and moves through the veins; it spreads in warm, wet conditions and on infected seed or transplants.

beginner: There's no real cure, so remove and destroy infected plants to keep it from spreading. Don't handle or brush against the plants while they're wet, because that spreads the bacteria.
seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Avoid working among plants when foliage is wet, since that moves the bacteria.

beginner: Begin with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, don't plant where cabbage-family crops grew recently, space plants for good airflow, and avoid overhead watering.
seasoned: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants (a hot-water seed treatment helps), rotate 2 to 3 years away from brassicas, give plants room for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and handling wet foliage.

beginner: Pale, sunken spots dotted with tiny black specks appear on the stem and leaves, and the base of the stem darkens and rots, so the plant may girdle and topple. It often arrives on infected seed.
seasoned: Pale, sunken lesions peppered with small black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) form on stems and leaves, and a dark, girdling canker at the stem base can rot the crown and lodge the plant; cankers may extend into the head.

beginner: A fungus that comes in on infected seed or plants and attacks the stem and leaves of cabbage-family crops. It spreads in wet weather and lingers in old plant debris.
seasoned: The fungus Phoma lingam (Leptosphaeria maculans) is chiefly seedborne and also survives in brassica debris; it spreads in cool, wet weather by splashing water and infects through wounds and pores.

beginner: There's no cure, so pull and destroy infected plants. The real fix is prevention: clean seed, rotation, and clearing away old cabbage-family debris.
seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Management is preventive, since the pathogen is carried on seed and in residue.

beginner: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, rotate away from cabbage-family crops for a few years, and clear away old brassica plants where the fungus survives.
seasoned: Use clean, certified, hot-water-treated seed and disease-free transplants, rotate 3 years away from brassicas, and bury or remove crop debris that carries the fungus over.

beginner: Whole plants turn a dull yellow-green, often more on one side, with leaves curling and dropping from the bottom up. Cut a stem and the water-carrying tissue inside is browned. It is worst in warm soil.
seasoned: A warm-season wilt: plants turn dull yellow-green (often one-sided), leaves curl, cup, and drop from the base up, and the vascular tissue in the stem browns. Stunting and death follow in susceptible varieties; symptoms resemble black rot but without the V-shaped marginal lesions.

beginner: A soil fungus that gets into the roots and plugs the plant's plumbing, so it yellows and wilts. It lives in the soil for years and is most active when the soil is warm, so it hits summer-grown cabbage hardest.
seasoned: The soilborne fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. conglutinans invades the roots and vascular system; it persists in soil for years and is most active in warm soil (roughly 80°F and up), so it most damages spring cabbage maturing into summer heat.

beginner: There's no cure once a plant is infected, so pull and destroy it. The reliable answer is to plant resistant (yellows-resistant) varieties.
seasoned: There is no cure for infected plants; remove and destroy them. Resistant varieties are the practical control, since the fungus is long-lived in soil.

beginner: Plant yellows-resistant varieties, which are widely available and the main control. Rotate away from cabbage-family crops, and avoid planting cabbage to mature in the hottest soil.
seasoned: Grow yellows-resistant (YR) varieties, which provide durable, effective resistance and are the standard control; rotate away from brassicas and avoid timing the crop to mature in the hottest soil.

beginner: Pale yellow blotches on top of the leaves, with fuzzy grayish growth on the underside, mostly in cool, damp weather. Bad cases discolor the leaves and can spot the head.
seasoned: Pale yellow patches form on the upper leaf surface with a fuzzy gray-white growth underneath, mainly in cool, damp weather; severe infection discolors the wrapper leaves and can blemish the head. Cabbage's cool, humid season overlaps the weather it likes.

beginner: A mold-like disease that loves cool, wet, humid weather and spreads through the air and water. Wet leaves and crowded plants make it worse.
seasoned: A fungus-like organism (Hyaloperonospora parasitica) that thrives in cool, wet, humid conditions and spreads by spores in water and air; long leaf wetness and crowded plantings favor it.

beginner: Open up the airflow so leaves can dry, remove the worst leaves, and use a copper spray if it's spreading. It's hard to stop once the weather stays damp.
seasoned: Improve airflow and let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high; the disease is hard to stop once humidity stays high.

beginner: Space plants so air moves between them, water at the soil instead of from above, and pick resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.
seasoned: Space plants for good air movement, water at the soil line rather than overhead, and choose resistant varieties where downy mildew is common.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 to 1.5 inches a week. Try to keep it steady, not dry-then-soaked.
seasoned: Give about 1 to 1.5 inches weekly, kept as even as possible, and ease off slightly right at maturity to avoid splitting.

beginner: Aim for roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week.
seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches per week (UMN: roughly 1 inch of rainfall a week is enough), more in hot, dry spells while heads are sizing up.

beginner: Water at the base of the plant rather than over the leaves.
seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose where possible to keep foliage dry and discourage leaf disease.

beginner: Lower leaves yellow and the plant looks soggy and limp.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and limp growth; cabbage dislikes waterlogged soil, which invites root maggots, clubroot, and crown rot in cold, wet ground.

beginner: Wilting leaves and small heads, and cracked, split heads if a dry spell is followed by a big drink of water.
seasoned: Wilting and stalled growth, then small, loose heads; and worst of all, a heavy watering or rain after a dry spell near maturity bursts the heads.

beginner: Keep the soil or tray damp while the seeds come up, without letting the surface dry out.
seasoned: Keep the seedbed or tray surface evenly moist through germination; brassica seed is shallow and should not dry mid-emergence.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly damp as they grow.
seasoned: Grow the seedlings on with steady, even moisture.

beginner: Water evenly, about 1 to 1.5 inches a week, as the outer leaves grow before the head forms.
seasoned: Keep even moisture as the plant builds its frame of wrapper leaves ahead of heading.

beginner: Keep the water steady while the head forms and fills. Even watering makes a firm, heavy cabbage.
seasoned: Even moisture matters most while heads form and fill; steady watering builds a solid, heavy head.

beginner: As the head gets full, water a little less. A big soak or heavy rain after a dry stretch makes a ready cabbage split open. If rain is coming, pick it or give the plant a gentle twist to slow it down.
seasoned: Ease off slightly as heads near maturity. A nearly full head that gets a sudden soak after a dry spell splits open; steady, moderate moisture avoids it. If heavy rain threatens a ready head, harvesting or giving the plant a twist to break some roots heads off the split.

beginner: Keep the water steady so the heads grow firm and do not crack. Big swings from dry to wet are what split cabbage.
seasoned: Even, steady moisture is the whole game with cabbage: it builds firm, solid heads and, just as important, prevents the splitting that a sudden flush of water causes near maturity.

beginner: Water steadily while the heads are forming and filling, and do not suddenly soak a nearly ripe head.
seasoned: Even moisture matters most while heads are forming and filling; this is also when a sudden change in watering will split a nearly mature head.

beginner: You can grow cabbage from transplants or sow the seeds right in the garden, especially for a fall crop. For spring, start seeds indoors about a month before planting out and set the plants out a few weeks before your last frost, since young cabbage handles cold well. For fall, start them in early to mid summer. Let homegrown seedlings get used to the outdoors over a week before planting.
seasoned: Cabbage is usually transplanted but can also be direct sown, especially for the fall crop. For spring, start seeds indoors about 4 to 6 weeks before set-out and transplant sturdy young plants out 2 to 4 weeks before the last frost, since cabbage transplants are cold-hardy. For fall, sow indoors or direct seed in early-to-mid summer and set out in mid-to-late summer to mature in cool fall weather. Set out stocky plants with 4 to 6 true leaves and harden them off over 7 to 10 days. Avoid setting out overly large or root-bound transplants into a cold spell, which can trigger bolting.

beginner: Other cabbage-family crops like broccoli, brussels sprouts, cauliflower, kale, and turnips.
seasoned: Other brassicas (broccoli, brussels sprouts, cauliflower, kale, collards, kohlrabi, turnip, radish, mustard), which share clubroot and the cabbage-family pests.

beginner: Don't plant cabbage or other cabbage-family crops in the same spot year after year. Waiting at least 3 years between them, and longer if you have had clubroot, helps avoid soil diseases.
seasoned: Rotate so cabbage and its brassica relatives do not return to the same ground for at least 3 years, and longer where clubroot is present (UMN advises a 7-year break where clubroot is known). Repeated same-family cropping builds soil-borne clubroot and Fusarium yellows, and holding soil pH near neutral also helps suppress clubroot.

beginner: A firm cabbage head will keep a week or two at room temperature, but it lasts far longer in the cold. Late storage types are made to keep for months.
seasoned: A solid cabbage head keeps for a week or two in a cool room, but quality is best cold. Cabbage is one of the great storage vegetables: late, dense storage types keep for months near freezing, which is the real advantage of the crop.

beginner: Store whole, unwashed heads in the fridge crisper, where a firm head keeps for several weeks. In a very cold, humid spot (right around freezing) late storage cabbage keeps for months. Keep it away from apples and other ripening fruit, which make it go off sooner.
seasoned: Refrigerate whole, unwashed heads with the wrapper leaves on; a solid head holds for several weeks to a couple of months in the crisper. For long storage, hold at 32°F to 34°F and 95% to 98% humidity, where dense late types keep 2 to 6 months (USU; Clemson up to 5 months). Keep cabbage away from ethylene-producing fruit, which yellows the leaves faster.

beginner: You can freeze cabbage if you blanch it first. Cut it up, boil it briefly (1 to 3 minutes), cool it in ice water, drain, and freeze; use it cooked. Cabbage is also great for making sauerkraut or kimchi, which keep a long time.
seasoned: Cabbage freezes after blanching: cut into wedges or shred, blanch about 1.5 minutes (shreds) to 3 minutes (wedges), cool quickly in ice water, drain, and freeze. Blanching halts the enzymes that cause off-flavors; frozen cabbage is best used cooked. Fresh cabbage is also the basis of fermented sauerkraut and kimchi for long keeping.

beginner: How long cabbage keeps depends on the type: late storage varieties are made to last for months somewhere cold and humid, while early types are for eating fresh within a few weeks. For long storage, leave a few outer leaves on, keep it cold and damp, and check now and then.
seasoned: Storage life depends heavily on type: dense, late storage varieties (Danish Ballhead, late flat Dutch types) are bred to hold for months in a root cellar or cold, humid fridge, while early, looser types are for fresh use within weeks. For cellar storage, harvest with a few wrapper leaves and the stem on, keep cold and humid, and check periodically for soft outer leaves.

beginner: Pick the type that fits your season. Early kinds like Golden Acre and Stonehead grow quickly for spring; later, denser kinds like Danish Ballhead are made to store for months in fall and winter. If you have had trouble with cabbage yellows (a soil disease), choose a yellows-resistant variety. Savoy cabbages have pretty crinkled leaves and are very cold-hardy, and red cabbages add color.
seasoned: Match the variety to the season and the purpose. Early types (Golden Acre, Early Jersey Wakefield, Stonehead) finish fast for spring and small heads; mid-season hybrids (Bravo, Market Prize, Rio Verde) give uniform, often yellows-resistant heads; late storage types (Danish Ballhead and late flat Dutch types) are the ones to grow for fall and long winter keeping. Where Fusarium yellows is a problem, choose a yellows-resistant (YR) variety, the main control for that disease. Savoy types are tender and cold-hardy for cooking; red types add color and hold well. Days-to-maturity figures are approximate and run from transplanting.

beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
seasoned: A rich, well-drained commercial potting mix high in organic matter.

beginner: Mix in compost and a slow-release fertilizer for steady feeding.
seasoned: Blend in compost and a slow-release balanced fertilizer; a single cabbage in a pot is a heavy feeder in a small soil volume.

beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check daily in warm weather and keep the water steady, since uneven watering cracks the heads.
seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; check moisture daily in heat and water before the mix dries, keeping it even to avoid splitting the head.

beginner: Feed a bit more often than in the ground, since watering washes nutrients out of pots.
seasoned: Container plants need more frequent feeding than in-ground ones because watering leaches nutrients.

beginner: Cabbage grows fine in a large pot. Use a container of at least 5 gallons, one plant per pot, and keep it well watered and fed. Compact early varieties like Golden Acre are the best fit. The main trick is steady watering so the head does not crack.
seasoned: Cabbage is a workable container crop, especially the compact early varieties. Use a pot of at least 5 gallons (10 is better) at least 10 inches deep, one plant per pot, in a rich, well-drained mix, and keep moisture and feeding steady, since a small soil volume runs out and uneven watering splits the head. Choose small, fast types (Golden Acre, Early Jersey Wakefield, Stonehead) over the big late storage kinds. Container-specific figures are modeled on general container-vegetable guidance plus the plant's size.

beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which keeps the head from cracking.
seasoned: A self-watering container suits cabbage well, since it smooths out the even moisture that keeps the head solid and uncracked.

beginner: Give one cabbage a wide pot that holds at least 5 gallons and is about 10 inches deep. A broad, sturdy pot holds water more evenly than a tall skinny one, which helps keep the head from cracking.

beginner: Cabbage handles the valley's swings well and rewards two plantings: an early spring crop for a quick harvest before the heat, then a fall crop set out in late summer that firms up as the weather cools, often the season's best cabbage. Give both crops a few weeks' head start before setting transplants out.
seasoned: Cabbage carries a genuine two-cycle calendar here per the UNLV/UNR Cooperative Extension Master Gardener planting chart and the belt's cool-season framework (University of Nevada, Reno Extension Fact Sheet FS-02-61): spring transplants set out in late winter mature before the desert's brutal summer heat, and fall transplants set out in late summer form firm heads as nights cool, generally the more reliable crop of the two.

beginner: Cabbage grows twice a year in St. George. Set plants out about February 15, USU Extension's St. George date, for heads by mid-May. USU's chart also lists cabbage as a documented fall crop with a wide planting window from May into mid-July; set the second round in from mid-June to mid-July so it heads up for an October harvest, well ahead of the frost that returns around November 1.
seasoned: USU Extension's St. George chart sets cabbage in the Group A (Hardy) band, spring set-out about February 15, heads firming up at about 85 days for a harvest through May. Cabbage is also one of USU's dated Special Plants for Fall Harvest, with an unusually wide documented planting window running from May 1 to July 15; the later half of that window, mid-June to mid-July, is used here so the second planting clears the spring harvest cleanly rather than overlapping it, heading up for an October harvest ahead of the November 1 average first frost.

beginner: Cabbage grows one big, round, solid head of tightly wrapped leaves at the center of the plant. There are green, red, and crinkly savoy types, some quick (about 2 months) and some late storage kinds (about 4 months). It likes cool weather, so it is grown in spring and again in fall, not in summer heat. Cabbage handles frost well, and late storage types keep for months somewhere cold. The main thing to watch is splitting: keep the watering even and pick the head as soon as it is firm so it does not crack.
seasoned: Cabbage is a cool-season brassica grown for the large, solid head of tightly wrapped leaves that forms at the center of the plant. It comes in early, mid, and late types maturing from about 60 to 120 days, in green, red, and crinkled savoy forms, and is grown as a spring crop and again as a fall crop in most regions, timed to head up in cool weather since heat gives loose heads and bolting. It is very cold-hardy, with mature heads tolerating frost down to about 20°F, and dense late storage types are among the best-keeping garden vegetables, holding for months in cold, humid storage. The crop's signature challenge is splitting: a solid head bursts if it takes up water too fast near maturity or is left standing too long.

beginner: Your cabbage is ready when the head is full-sized and firm and solid when you squeeze it. Cut it off at the base with a sharp knife. Pick it as soon as it is firm, because a ripe head left sitting will crack, especially after rain. If you are not ready, give the plant a quarter turn to slow it down.
seasoned: Cut the head when it is full-sized, firm, and solid to a squeeze, about 60 to 120 days from transplanting depending on the type. Slice it off at the base with a sharp knife, leaving a few wrapper leaves for protection. Harvest promptly, since a mature head left in the ground will split, especially after rain; to hold a ripe head, give the plant a quarter turn or a slight lift to shear roots and slow water uptake.

beginner: Before planting, mix plenty of compost into a rich, well-drained bed and check that the soil is not too acidic. Try not to plant where you grew other cabbage-family crops in the last few years, since that spreads soil diseases. Plan to water evenly, which keeps the heads firm and crack-free.
seasoned: Work plenty of compost into a fertile, well-drained but moisture-retentive bed before planting and confirm pH is near 6.0 to 7.0, liming acidic ground well ahead where clubroot is a concern. Because clubroot and Fusarium yellows build in the soil, choose a bed where no cole crop has grown for at least 3 years, and set up to water evenly, since steady moisture is what builds a solid, split-free head.
